messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Shutting stan up?
parts:
Hey all,

I'm currently running a simulation study comparing different modeling techniques for a certain kind of data. The stan model in question is run 10,000 times for 240 different data conditions (varying in N, skewness, variance difference between groups, and imbalance of N between groups, so, basically, lots of simulations).

To save time, I'm using stan's optimizer and the hessians for some approximations, and I promise it makes sense in this case.

However, I've noticed that the optimizer will occasionally hang, so it's using 100% CPU but not progressing or providing output. I can stop the process, restart the condition, and get the 10,000 simulations for that condition within a few seconds.

I can't figure out why this is, but I /suspect/ it may be due to a gigantic number of messages that stan is sending (e.g., warnings about initial values not being evaluated, occasional problems evaluating the density on an optimizing stage).

Is there any way I can test this by truly shutting up stan? No messages, no warnings, no nothing; just the final converged output (and it always converges, so it doesn't appear to be a convergence issue)?

It's /really/ obnoxious having to hover over the rstudio output waiting for the optimizer to hang, killing the processes, restarting the sim after the last complete condition, etc.

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Re: Shutting stan up?
parts:
False alarm! It's failing due to occasional infinite loops caused by bad random inits. I used init=0 and the issues seem to have gone away.

That said, it /would/ be nice to shut stan up sometimes; it can flood the output window and nearly crashes my browser when using my rstudio server from my [crappy] laptop.
I've tried everything; sink('/dev/null'), the R functions for suppressing messages/warnings/output/etc, stan still finds a way to say something on my output window which can be an issue when you're running 10,000 models * 240 conditions.
